#1  Hurricane Isaias · AL092026 · Adv 8 85 mph

Type & strengthHurricane Isaias — 85 mph (Cat 1), 975 mb
ISAIAS STRONGER
Additional strengthening is expected through early Friday, and Isaias should remain a dangerous hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast Friday night. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 15 miles (30 km) from the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 90 miles (150 km).

about 170 mi N of Progreso Mexico
about 380 mi S of the Mouth of the Mississippi River
about 190 mi N of Merida, Mexico (computed from the official position, not an NHC statement)

Key hazards
  • Storm Surge: The combination of a dangerous storm surge and the tide will cause normally dry areas near the coast to be flooded by rising waters moving inland from the shoreline. The water could reach the following heights above ground somewhere in the indicated areas if the peak surge occurs at the time of high tide... Ocean Springs, MS to Indian Pass, FL...5-7 ft Mobile Bay...5-7 ft Indian Pass, FL to Steinhatchee River, FL...4-6 ft Mouth of the Mississippi River, LA to Ocean Springs, MS...3-5 ft Steinhatchee River, FL to Suwannee River, FL...3-5 ft Suwannee River, FL to Yankeetown, FL...2-4 ft The deepest water will occur along the immediate coast near and to the east of the landfall location, where the surge will be accompanied by large and dangerous waves. Surge-related flooding depends on the relative timing of the surge and the tidal cycle, and can vary greatly over short distances. For information specific to your area, please see products issued by your local National Weather Service forecast office. For a complete depiction of areas at risk of storm surge inundation, please see the National Weather Service Peak Storm Surge Graphic, available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?peakSurge.
  • Wind: Hurricane conditions are expected within the Hurricane Warning area Friday night into early Saturday, with tropical storm conditions beginning on Friday. Tropical storm conditions are expected in the warning areas on Friday and Friday night. Gusty winds are possible in portions of the Yucatan Peninsula today.
  • Rainfall: Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches through Thursday across coastal portions of the eastern Bay of Campeche with isolated higher amounts possible in the states of Campeche and western Yucatan. From Friday through the weekend, Isaias is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 3 to 7 inches across the central U.S. Gulf Coast extending from far southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Big Bend region. Localized totals up to 15 inches are possible, particularly within banding across the Florida Panhandle and Big Bend. Rainfall amounts of 1 to 3 inches, with localized amounts up to 5 inches, are possible across much of the Southeast as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas. Flash and urban flooding is possible across the region, with considerable impacts possible across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwestern Georgia. River flooding is also expected, some of which could be significant. For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Tropical Storm Isaias, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?rainqpf and the Flash Flood Risk graphic at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ero.
  • Tornadoes: Isolated tornadoes will be possible Friday night in coastal areas of Alabama and the Florida Panhandle and far southwestern Georgia. The tornado threat will continue Saturday for eastern Alabama, Georgia and northern Florida.
  • Surf: Swells will affect the western and northern portions of the Yucatan Peninsula beginning later today and spread northward toward the Gulf Coast on Friday. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office. A depiction of rip current risk for the United States can be found at: hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ripCurrents

Key hazards
  • Wind: Hurricane conditions are possible within the hurricane watch area by Saturday night, with tropical storm conditions beginning on Saturday. Tropical storm conditions are possible within the tropical storm watch area beginning Friday.
  • Rainfall: Simon is expected to produce rainfall totals of 8 to 15 inches over portions of southwestern Mexico, with isolated maximum totals between 15 and 25 inches possible across portions of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco through Sunday. This rainfall may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Simon, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_ep5.shtml?rainqpf.
  • Storm Surge: A dangerous storm surge is possible along the immediate coast near and to the east of where the center makes landfall. Near the coast,the surge will be accompanied by large and destructive waves.
  • Surf: Swells generated by Simon will affect portions of the coast of southwestern and west-central Mexico during the next few days. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office.

Work with us — Advertise & Sponsor

FR-STORM is a free, independent hurricane dashboard for the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts, refreshed every 3 hours from official NHC / NWS / JTWC data. If you'd like to support it or reach its readers, these are the options:

  • Sponsor this dashboard — your name or logo shown here as “Sponsored by…”, plus a line in the page footer.
  • Advertising placement (banner or card) — a clearly labelled banner or card in this section only.
  • Storm-season local business sponsorship (Gulf / Atlantic coast) — for local businesses that want to support hurricane-season readiness along the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts.
  • Other partnership / service offer — data, tools, services or other ideas.

Ground rules: sponsor and advertising content appears only in this section and the page footer, always labelled “Sponsor”. It is never placed inside the storm cards, maps, alerts or the official NHC / NWS information, and sponsors have no say in the storm information. Pricing and audience details are shared on request — none are published here.

Sources & how this was made

Why this page exists

It is a free, independent hurricane check focused on the US Gulf and Atlantic coasts. It puts the threat first: is anything likely to affect land within 72 hours, where and when — then the rest of the Atlantic, Pacific and West Pacific for context.

How it is built

  1. Every 3 hours a scheduled job runs refresh_storm_dash.sh on a private workstation.
  2. Python scripts download the official products listed below straight from NOAA's National Hurricane Center (NHC/CPHC), the National Weather Service (NWS) and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) — text advisories, outlooks and the NHC GIS shapefiles (cone, track, forecast points, past track, outlook areas, watch/warning lines).
  3. The scripts rank systems by threat to the US / Florida, draw the static maps, and build this page. The interactive map's shapes are embedded in the page at build time (no live data calls), so it is a snapshot as of the pulled time shown.
  4. The page is published to GitHub Pages (a static web host) and checked live after each refresh.

Translation, units and time zones

Any language: the language picker at the top uses the Google Website Translator — this is machine translation by Google, done in your browser, and it can be wrong. The English text is the official version (copied from NHC / NWS / JTWC); if anything is unclear, use the English page or the official NHC products. Storm names, advisory numbers, storm IDs, coordinates and source URLs are marked do not translate. If the translator widget can't load, the Open translated page link opens a Google Translate copy of this page instead. Your language choice is remembered in this browser (localStorage) and re-applied on every refresh.

Units and times: NHC publishes winds in mph and knots, pressure in millibars (mb = hPa) and times in Eastern Time. The unit buttons (wind mph / km/h / kt, distance mi / km, pressure mb / hPa / inHg) and the extra local-time display are converted in your browser from those official values; the default is US units for US-English browsers and metric elsewhere.

Official vs. calculated

  • Official (copied from NHC/NWS/JTWC): storm positions, winds, pressure, movement, forecast points and times, cones, outlook areas and formation odds, watches/warnings, wind-speed probabilities, NWS alerts and discussion text.
  • Calculated by this dashboard (not official): plain-language positions ("about 400 mi W of…"), estimated coast-crossing times interpolated between NHC forecast points, threat ranking and the CLEAR / MONITOR / WATCH / WARNING status labels (those labels follow NWS watches/warnings when any exist).
  • Duplicate check: when an outlook invest (e.g. Invest AL92) becomes an advisory storm (e.g. TD Nine, AL09), the old invest entry is dropped automatically. Nothing needed dropping this run.
  • Fetch problems this run: none — every source above downloaded and parsed.

Limitations

  • This is not an official warning source. It can be up to 3 hours old, a download can fail, and parsing can be wrong. Always follow the National Hurricane Center (nhc.noaa.gov), your local National Weather Service office (weather.gov) and your county emergency management (evacuation zones, shelters: ready.gov/hurricanes).
  • The cone shows where the storm's center will probably go — not how big the storm is. Surge, wind and rain often reach far outside it.
  • Formation odds are chances a depression or storm forms, not landfall odds. Disturbances have no official track until NHC starts advisories.
  • Times are converted to Eastern Time (your local time can be shown next to them). GTWO outlook GIS stamp: Thu Oct 8, 7:45 AM ET.
  • Translations are machine-made by Google and may be wrong; the English NHC/NWS wording is the official text.

Odds are NHC tropical-cyclone formation chances, not landfall chances. NHC winds are 1-min sustained as published (mph); JTWC knots are converted to mph. "Computed" items (distances, plain-language positions, interpolated coast crossings) are Free Runner calculations from official positions, not official statements. For decisions use hurricanes.gov, your local NWS office (weather.gov) and your county emergency management.
